I've been working this land for fifty years. My body isn't what it was, and with just my wife and me, I can't push too hard. But I know these fields. I know when they're thirsty and when they've had enough. Let me think through what I'll do.

**Wheat (October planting, June harvest):**
All 4.1 mu goes to wheat first. I'll buy improved seed from the county seed station — not the old varieties my father used, the newer ones yield better, and the village extension station has been pushing them for years. They work. For fertilizer, I'll put down diammonium phosphate and urea as base before planting, then topdress urea in spring at jointing. I've learned over the years not to put too much — it wastes money and makes the stalks fall over. Irrigation: I'll do the winter freeze irrigation in November to help the roots, then water again at jointing, and again at grain fill. Three times. Herbicides after emergence, then one spray for aphids and powdery mildew in May — two pesticide passes total. My neighbor hires a rotary tiller machine after maize harvest each autumn; I'll do the same.

**Maize (June planting, October harvest):**
Right after I sell the wheat, I plant maize on the same 4.1 mu. Hybrid seed —郑单 958 or whatever the seed shop is stocking this year. Hybrids are the only sensible choice now. I direct-seed without tilling — saves money and time, and the soil is already loose from wheat. I'll water at planting if it's dry, and again at silking. Two irrigations is usually enough with our wells. Fertilizer same approach — base and topdress. Pesticide twice, once for weeds, once for borers.

**At my age**, I keep things simple. I'm not experimenting.
